sentences.text: The animal belongs to the genus Megaraptor, with the only named species being Megaraptor namunhuaiquii.
Its skull was long, low, and slender, based primarily on a juvenile specimen that Fernando Novas estimated to be around 8 meters long.
The first finger claw measured 35 cm in total length, while the third finger claw was only 6.5 cm long, showing the large claw belonged to the first finger, not the second toe.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the length at 8 meters and weight at 1 tonne in 2010.
The genus was described by Fernando E. Novas in 1998, following the discovery of the type specimen, consisting of fragmentary limb bones, in January 1996.
Fossils were found in the Portezuelo Formation in Patagonia, Argentina, where Megaraptor lived approximately 98 million years ago in what is now South America.
Megaraptor lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically from the Turonian to the Coniacian stages, in an environment that was a fluvial deposit with a humid climate.

While it was initially suggested to use claws to open carcasses, active predation is now generally favored, perhaps using large hand claws to grab prey and pull them toward its chest to be dispatched by its jaws.

Researchers initially suggested Megaraptor was a basal tetanuran rather than a coelurosaur, but the clade Megaraptora was erected in 2012 to include Megaraptor namunhuaiquii and its closest relatives.

The assignment of the juvenile specimen to M. namunhuaiquii has been questioned, even by its original describer, as a 2025 paper noted morphological inconsistencies between the juvenile and larger specimens, questioning their referral to the same genus. Researchers suggest the referral to a single genus may have been driven by the fact that specimens were found at the same locality.

In 2025, researchers used allometry to suggest that a fully mature Megaraptor skull would likely have been deeper, more robust, and had proportionally smaller eye sockets than the known juvenile specimen.
